title: Childhood type 1 diabetes: an environment-wide association study across England.
ehr_evidence: We obtained type 1 diabetes data from National Health Service (NHS) Digital hospital episode statistics (HES) records.
summary: Ecological EnWAS assessing associations between 53 demographic and environmental factors and childhood type 1 diabetes incidence across England.
key_findings: Overall incidence was 21.2 (95% CI 20.9, 21.6) per 100,000 children aged 0–9 years.
15 of 53 factors were significantly associated with incidence after multiple testing.
Multivariable ecological regression showed the living environment domain of IMD was inversely associated with risk (RR 0.995; 95% CrI 0.991, 0.998).
Radon potential class was positively associated with risk (RR 1.044; 95% CrI 1.015, 1.074).
Air pollutants, lead in soil, overcrowding, population density, and ethnicity showed significant unadjusted associations but were not significant in the multivariable model.
captured_features: environmental and demographic variables at LAD level
study_design: ecological environment-wide association study with disease mapping and multivariable ecological regression
exposure_domain: environmental and demographic factors (air pollution, radon, land use, meteorological, socioeconomic deprivation, ethnicity, overcrowding)
limitations: ecological study design using aggregate LAD-level counts
potential ecological bias and residual confounding by unmeasured individual-level factors
temporal mismatch between some exposure and health data
loss of spatial granularity due to aggregation
high intercorrelation among variables prevented full mutual adjustment
data_availability_statement: The majority of the demographic and environmental factors included in the study were derived from Crown copyright data and are available via the links provided in the text and references. HES data are available via NHS Digital on application with appropriate ethics and governance permissions; we do not hold data provider, ethics or governance permissions to share these health data with third parties.
